lessons.title: Three documented cases and their limits
lessons.subtitle: COMPAS, Amazon's experiment and Gender Shades

sections.title: COMPAS: different fairness measures
sections.content:
COMPAS is a risk-assessment instrument whose scores were used in parts of the US justice system as one input among others. In 2016, ProPublica examined more than 7,000 scores assigned in Broward County, Florida, and compared them with later recorded arrests. The publication reported, among other findings, that Black defendants who were not arrested again during the observation period had been incorrectly classified as high risk more often than comparable white defendants. (Source: Angwin et al., ProPublica, 2016)

Northpointe disputed the assessment and argued that scores were similarly calibrated for both groups within risk bands. Different criteria were therefore being compared: similar calibration within a score and similar error rates between groups. Chouldechova showed that, where base rates differ, such criteria generally cannot be satisfied at the same time unless prediction is perfect. (Source: Chouldechova, A. (2017). Fair prediction with disparate impact. Big Data, 5(2))

The analysis establishes a disparity under ProPublica's error-rate measure. By itself, it does not establish which data or design choice caused that disparity.
sections.keyTakeaway: The COMPAS dispute used different fairness measures. A model can be similarly calibrated within risk bands while producing different error rates between groups.

sections.title: Amazon: an abandoned recruitment experiment
sections.content:
In 2018, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the project, on an internal experimental Amazon system for ranking resumes. The models had been developed using applications submitted over a ten-year period; many came from men. One model penalised terms including "women's" and the names of two women's colleges. (Source: Dastin, J., Reuters, October 2018)

The team removed identifiable gender-related signals but, according to the report, could not guarantee that the system would not use other proxy features. Amazon disbanded the project team by early 2017. The company told Reuters that recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates.

The case documents a development risk: historical application data can contain earlier selection patterns. Whether and how a model adopts those patterns also depends on the target, features, validation and deployment decision. The report does not establish a hiring decision caused by this tool.
sections.keyTakeaway: Reuters documented an internal experiment with gender-related ranking effects. Amazon said recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates.

sections.title: Gender Shades: an audit of commercial gender classification
sections.content:
In 2018, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ on how they classified binary gender from facial images. This was gender classification, not identifying a person through facial recognition. (Source: Buolamwini, J. & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender Shades. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 81)

For lighter-skinned men, the highest reported error rate was 0.8 percent. For darker-skinned women, error rates reached 34.7 percent depending on the system. The study therefore found substantial intersectional performance differences in the tested products.

The authors separately examined the demographic composition of two widely used benchmarks and documented representation skews. Without access to each system's training data, however, this does not establish that those benchmarks or one particular data distribution caused each vendor's errors.

The supported finding is the measured performance disparity under the study design. Its cause, transfer to other tasks and current product performance require separate evidence.
sections.keyTakeaway: Gender Shades measured error rates of up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women and at most 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men in commercial gender classification. It did not prove a particular training-data cause for every vendor.

quiz.questionText: Which finding did ProPublica report in its COMPAS analysis?

answerOptions.text: The system was technically defective and produced arbitrary results
White defendants were twice as likely as Black defendants to be wrongly classified as posing a high risk of reoffending
Under ProPublica's error-rate measure, Black defendants without a subsequent arrest were incorrectly classified as high risk more often than comparable white defendants
The system was perfectly fair, but the dataset was too small

quiz.explanation: ProPublica reported different error rates. Northpointe pointed to calibration within risk bands. Chouldechova's analysis explains why calibration and equal error rates can generally be incompatible when base rates differ.

quiz.questionText: What is established about Amazon's experimental recruitment tool?

answerOptions.text: The model was deliberately programmed to do so
Reuters reported gender-related ranking effects; Amazon said recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates
The system could not identify applicants' gender
Applications from women were actually weaker

quiz.explanation: Reuters described an internal experiment that penalised terms including "women's". Amazon said recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates. The report therefore establishes a development risk, not a particular hiring decision.

quiz.questionText: What did Gender Shades find about commercial gender classification?

answerOptions.text: The systems identified all faces with similar accuracy
Only less expensive systems had bias problems
At almost 12 percent, darker-skinned men had the highest error rate among the four groups studied
The highest error rate was 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men and reached 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women depending on the system

quiz.explanation: Gender Shades tested binary gender classification by IBM, Microsoft and Face++. It measured substantial intersectional performance differences. It was not a study of person identification and did not prove a particular training-data cause for every vendor.

lessons.title: Ethics at three levels: technology, organisations and society
lessons.subtitle: How to allocate responsibility without diluting it

sections.title: Level 1: technology
sections.content:
At the technical level, examine system performance, error distribution and limitations.

Attribution methods such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) or LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) estimate, under chosen model, reference and perturbation assumptions, how input features contributed to an output. They do not show causation and do not automatically provide a complete explanation of the decision process.

A bias audit can compare error or selection rates across meaningfully defined groups. Its validity requires suitable targets, denominators, samples and uncertainty reporting. For high-risk AI systems, Article 9 governs a risk-management system. Article 10 contains data and data-governance requirements and, where relevant, examination of possible biases. Article 15 addresses accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Whether these duties already apply to a particular system depends on its classification, the operator's role and the current application date.

Technical tests can expose risks. They do not decide whether a use is lawful or socially acceptable.
sections.keyTakeaway: Attribution, group metrics and robustness tests answer different questions. No single metric explains causation, fairness and permissibility at once.

sections.title: Level 2: organisations
sections.content:
At the organisational level, every deployment needs a named purpose, a responsible role, approval criteria and a documented escalation route.

Where the relevant high-risk provisions apply, Article 12 requires a system to be technically capable of automatic logging. Under Article 26(6), deployers generally retain automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months unless other Union or national law provides a different period. The information available depends on the system and the deployer's actual access.

An internal review body can be useful, but an 'ethics board' is not mandated in every case. What matters is expertise, decision authority, documented approval and an incident process. Article 87 refers reporting of infringements of the AI Regulation and protection of reporting persons to Directive (EU) 2019/1937; the directive's scope and national law still require assessment.
sections.keyTakeaway: Logging capability, retention and internal approval are separate requirements. Their scope depends on system category, role and application date.

sections.title: Level 3: society
sections.content:
At the societal level, permissible purposes, rights and oversight routes are set. The AI Regulation, data-protection law, equal-treatment law and fundamental-rights requirements can apply in parallel and answer different questions.

Article 22(1) GDPR concerns decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect a person. Article 22(2) contains exceptions. For cases under paragraph 2(a) and (c), paragraph 3 requires at least the opportunity to obtain human intervention, express one's point of view and contest the decision. For relevant automated decision-making, Articles 13, 14 and 15 contain information duties or access rights concerning the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences. This is not a blanket entitlement to source code or an explanation for every algorithm.

For a significant decision, assess four points separately: Was it solely automated? What effect did it have? Could an exception apply? Which information and safeguards are available?
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 22 GDPR concerns solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects and contains exceptions. Safeguards and information rights must be assessed precisely under Articles 13 to 15 and Article 22.

quiz.questionText: Which retention duty can Article 26(6) impose on deployers of high-risk AI systems?

answerOptions.text: Send a monthly report to the EU AI Office
Generally retain automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, subject to other applicable law
Make every algorithm publicly accessible
Establish an internal ethics board

quiz.explanation: Where the provisions apply, Article 12 requires the technical capability for automatic logging. Article 26(6) generally requires the deployer to retain logs under its control for at least six months unless other law provides a different period.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about Article 22 GDPR is correct?

answerOptions.text: It creates a right to demand the deletion of all personal data
Article 22 prohibits every use of an algorithm in a decision
Article 22 automatically creates a complete right to see the source code for every AI output
Article 22 protects against solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; its exceptions and the required safeguards must be assessed

quiz.explanation: Article 22(1) concerns decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects. Paragraph 2 provides exceptions. For contractual necessity or explicit consent, paragraph 3 requires at least human intervention, the opportunity to express one's point of view and the ability to contest the decision; further information rights arise under Articles 13 to 15.

quiz.questionText: What is a central difference between the technical and societal levels of AI ethics?

answerOptions.text: Societal measures are ineffective because technology moves faster than policy
Technical measures alone determine the purposes for which an AI system may be used
The technical level has clear answers, whereas the societal level has none
Technology can measure and reduce bias but cannot decide which purposes AI may serve; that is a social and political decision

quiz.explanation: Technical measures such as explainability, bias measurement and robustness matter, but they do not resolve political questions. A technically optimised facial recognition system can still be used for mass surveillance. Society, not technology, decides whether that use is permitted.

lessons.title: Three checks for real AI deployments
lessons.subtitle: Data, responsibility and oversight route

sections.title: Check 1: separate data from the target
sections.content:
Historical data can contain earlier inequalities, measurement errors or selection decisions. It does not follow automatically that every model trained on those data reproduces the same disparity. The outcome also depends on sampling, labels, features, target, optimisation, thresholds and deployment context.

Do not ask only where the data came from. Also ask: Who is represented? What counts as the correct outcome? Which errors are measured for which groups? Was performance tested in the actual deployment context?

The COMPAS, Amazon and Gender Shades cases concern different problems. They cannot be reduced to the single formula 'bad training data'.
sections.keyTakeaway: Assess data origin, target, error metric and deployment context separately. Historical data can contain disparities, but do not determine the outcome on their own.

sections.title: Check 2: map the role to the duty
sections.content:
'The AI decided' identifies neither a responsible organisation nor a legal basis. The AI Regulation assigns duties according to actual role and conduct: Article 16 contains provider duties, Article 22 duties for authorised representatives, Article 23 for importers, Article 24 for distributors and Article 26 for deployers. Article 25 governs cases in which another operator is treated as the provider.

This role allocation is not a blanket statement about liability or about who caused a discriminatory outcome. Data-protection, equal-treatment, employment or civil law may also apply.

For the individual case, document: Who provides the system? Who determines the purpose and deployment? Who makes or confirms the decision? Which provision attaches to that conduct?
sections.keyTakeaway: Assign the actual role before the specific duty. Article 16 and Articles 22 to 26 govern different operators; they do not create one blanket responsible party.

sections.title: Check 3: use a traceable oversight route
sections.content:
Use a fixed process for verifiable cases:

1. Document the purpose, responsible role, data source and human decision point.
2. For a significant automated decision, determine whether it was solely automated, what effect it had, which exception might apply and which information or safeguards are available.
3. For suspected synthetic media, preserve the original source and check provenance and context using the process from Block 2.
4. Record the finding, uncertainty and next responsible route separately.

For independent context, AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org), the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org) founded by Joy Buolamwini, and netzpolitik.org publish investigations into algorithmic systems, bias and digital regulation.
sections.keyTakeaway: A defensible oversight route documents purpose, role, data, decision, finding and uncertainty. It replaces assumptions with verifiable steps.

quiz.questionText: Which statement precisely describes the relationship between training data and model effects?

answerOptions.text: Because AI developers deliberately want to build discriminatory models
Because models always use too little training data, regardless of its composition
Because individual developers directly program their personal preferences into the model without realising it
Historical data can contain inequalities; model effects also depend on the target, features, testing and deployment

quiz.explanation: Historical data can reflect earlier inequalities. Whether they produce a harmful model effect also depends on selection, labels, target, modelling, thresholds, evaluation and deployment.

quiz.questionText: How does the AI Regulation allocate duties along the value chain?

answerOptions.text: Only the original AI developer
Nobody, because AI systems act independently
Only the market surveillance authority in the relevant EU Member State

By actual role: notably providers under Article 16, authorised representatives under Article 22, importers under Article 23, distributors under Article 24 and deployers under Article 26; Article 25 governs role changes

quiz.explanation: The duties appear in different articles and attach to the actual role. Article 25 can cause an operator to be treated as a provider. This allocation does not replace separate analysis of liability, data protection or equal treatment.

quiz.questionText: Which organisation founded by Joy Buolamwini conducts research and education on algorithmic bias?

answerOptions.text: AlgorithmWatch
netzpolitik.org
Data & Society Research Institute
Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org)

quiz.explanation: Joy Buolamwini founded the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org), which researches harms and inequities in algorithmic systems and provides education. AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org) examines algorithmic decision systems in Europe.
